source_text: Yeah, so I'm thinking this is a kind of scattering theory problem.  We put a real problem in on one side.  In the middle, it might bounce around inside the tech world for a while, with handoffs, factories, verification, etc., and then out the other side comes a concrete solution of some kind to a real problem.  For example, consider Doordash or delivery.  "We bring food to your house" solves a real human problem.  Inside, no doubt, there's lots of tech involved, and as Doordash improves its operations, even more tech.  But is it on the way to solving real human needs better or faster?

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) The scattering picture works for this. It gives a test for every tool on the list: does it change what comes out, or only how things bounce around inside? I've recorded it in the mission as §3.3 (`7ca2b4d`).

🈖 ("is it on the way to solving real human needs better or faster?") In scattering theory the internal detail matters only through what comes out. A tool earns its place if you can trace a path from the bounce it changes to a change in an out-state. By that test, most of group A (Mastra, Smithers, the memory databases) improves bounces. Whether that ever reaches anyone's dinner depends on the factory around it, and the tool alone can't tell you.

🈕 (DoorDash) The example adds one thing: there's more than one out-channel. The customer gets food: how fast, how cheap, whether it's the right order. The same process also has out-channels for couriers (pay, hours) and for restaurants (margin). Extra tech inside can make the customer's channel better or faster while making the couriers' worse. So "better for whom?" has to be part of how the out-state is described.

㊟ (a case already in the data) The customer-stories research has an example where the bounces cancel out. Judgment Labs' clients found that reviewing the agent's output took up the time the agent had saved. Each step was carried out faithfully, and nothing changed at the output. So fidelity at each step, in the T8 sense, doesn't add up to an end-to-end gain.

🈕 (War Machine) In this picture the R-nodes are internal bounces. "Grounded in how an organisation works" would then mean the War Machine's observations (R2) come from the organisation's out-channels, not from its own internal steps. That's a test you could apply to the current validation work.

🈰 (next) When the remaining customer-story agents report back, I'll write each client problem in this form:
- the in-state, as the client states it
- the out-channels, and who is on each one
- a measurable out-state for each channel
- which bounces each tool touches

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
(the sort) Five groups:
- **A. Tech for tech people (~36):** Mastra, Smithers, Cotal, Reticle, the memory DBs, and others. The buyer is a developer with a developer's problem.
- **B. One non-technical worker's task (~5):** Solid, Hyperbound, Voiskey, MiniMax Agent, o-machine. The client's problem is visible here, but there's no model of the organisation.
- **C. Capturing an expert's know-how (2):** ZooWork, Cognisee.
- **D. Making an organisation's working visible (~5):**
  - Scribe Optimize: what employees actually do, mined from their clicks.
  - Agentic Fabriq: whose authority an agent acts under.
  - AIUC-1: what a buyer or insurer can rely on.
  - Proof-of-Control: what outsiders can check.
  - p2r: each participant's own contribution.
- **E. Not products:** Plank, Tatras, Immersive Commons, atproto/Germ.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("grounded in the way an actual organisation works") Your distinction puts the War Machine closest to D, with one difference. D sells the record of how the organisation works, and A sells the factory. None of the D vendors builds a factory, and none of the A vendors models the organisation. A factory grounded in an organisation needs both, and that combination is where the War Machine sits. In SVO terms, A has one developer as its subject, B and C have one worker or expert, and D has several people holding intents that may conflict. D is also where the "human" problems live, like your manager who doesn't listen. So that filter will matter most for D-type clients.

previous_reply_acts.text: (next) Once the customer stories come back, I'll write the concrete client problems as triples and sort each one into human, tooling or mixed. That should answer your earlier question about why some verbs are more interesting than others.
